name: Vaseline on teeth (pageant trick)

lead: Contestants and photo subjects are reported to rub a thin layer of petroleum jelly over the front teeth before smiling for a long stretch. The slick layer is said to keep the upper lip from catching on dry teeth and to stop lipstick from marking the enamel.
The payoff is a smile that holds longer and looks cleaner on camera. The practice is documented through pageant accounts and beauty features rather than clinical research.

paras: People apply a very thin film to the visible front teeth shortly before an event or shoot, usually alongside lipstick. It is used for occasions rather than daily wear.

Petroleum jelly is generally regarded as low-risk in small swallowed amounts, but a writer who tried it noted that you will ingest some. Dentists have not published guidance endorsing it for teeth, and it is not a whitening product.

angle.text: A slick layer on the teeth lets the lip move freely over them and keeps lipstick off the enamel. It is used for events and photos to keep a smile looking even.

lead: The petroleum-jelly trick is a pageant and photo-shoot habit in which a thin layer of Vaseline or similar jelly is smeared on the teeth to make a long smile easier and tidier.

Accounts from the pageant world give two purposes: preventing the lips from sticking to dry teeth during extended smiling, and preventing dark or pigmented lipstick from staining the teeth. Miss World Philippines 2019 Michelle Dee described the lipstick-protection use on a Philippine TV show, saying a thin layer would prevent staining.[1] A beauty writer who tried it for a photoshoot reported that her lips did not stick to her teeth.[2]
No clinical research on the practice was found; it is documented through beauty features and personal accounts.

paras: Reports describe a very thin application to the front teeth just before smiling. Pageant sites say it helps contestants hold a smile on stage without the lip catching, and Michelle Dee has said it protects teeth from lipstick staining.[1]

The Guardian-sourced account summarised by search coverage says the writer found it made smiling easier but noted she would swallow some, so it suits occasional events.[2] Some pageant-oriented sites also say it brightens teeth; dental-focused sources say it may add shine but does not whiten.[2]
